title: Association of alcohol consumption with selected cardiovascular disease outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis

claims.statement: In adults without heart disease when they joined prospective cohort studies, mostly in high-income countries, drinking a little compared with not drinking is associated with less coronary heart disease, but how much less depends on who is counted as not drinking, and no paper read gives absolute risks, so the ratios cannot be turned into numbers out of 100. Against non-drinkers as each study defined them (in most studies people not drinking at the start, including former drinkers), people who drank had pooled relative risks of 0.71 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.77) for new coronary heart disease (29 studies) and 0.75 (0.68 to 0.81) for coronary death (31 studies); at 2.5 to 14.9 g of ethanol a day (up to about one drink, counted as 12.5 g where a study gave no grams) the figures were 0.75 (0.65 to 0.88) and 0.79 (0.73 to 0.86), below 2.5 g a day 0.96 (0.86 to 1.06) and 0.92 (0.80 to 1.06), and at every higher intake, up to more than 60 g a day, 0.66 to 0.79; 8 of the 84 cohort reports gave only unadjusted estimates (Ronksley et al., 2011). In the 7 to 9 studies that compared with lifetime abstainers the figures were similar (0.73, 0.61 to 0.88; 0.75, 0.66 to 0.85), and former drinkers had more coronary deaths (1.31, 1.02 to 1.68; against non-drinkers in the paper's table, against people who drank in its text). A review that compared only with lifetime abstainers and kept men, women, deaths and new cases apart (Roerecke & Rehm, 2012; 24 studies) found lower point estimates at about one drink of 12 g a day in all four groups, but men's coronary deaths were not clearly lower at about one or two drinks a day (0.89, 0.79 to 1.00; 0.86, 0.73 to 1.02) and women's were not lower at about two drinks (1.03, 0.84 to 1.27); with all 44 studies, including those that combined men and women or deaths and new cases, every estimate at about one to three drinks a day was lower (0.62 to 0.81), and occasional drinking (less than weekly, or under 2.5 g a day) was not associated with coronary risk in any group. Of 23 conditions in the GBD 2016 curves fitted to 592 studies, only ischaemic heart disease showed a significant dip, lowest at 0.83 drinks of 10 g a day in men (relative risk 0.86, 95% uncertainty interval 0.80 to 0.96) and 0.92 in women (0.82, 0.72 to 0.95). Self-reported drinking showed the same dip in Chinese men (Millwood et al., 2019) and in UK Biobank, where allowing for smoking, body mass index, physical activity, cooked vegetable and red meat intake and self-rated health removed the statistically clear difference at moderate intake (more than 8.4 to 15.4 US drinks of 14 g a week) and, read approximately from the paper's figure, reduced but did not remove it at light intake (Biddinger et al., 2022). Whether alcohol causes the lower risk is disputed: in the same team's earlier review, cited second-hand, former drinkers had more coronary deaths than lifetime abstainers (men 1.25, women 1.54), and in men drinking 60 g a day or more the lower risk seen against current non-drinkers (0.75, 0.63 to 0.89) was not seen against lifetime abstainers (1.00, 0.74 to 1.36; Roerecke & Rehm, 2014); genetic studies do not find the lower risk (see the answer on gene studies). Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Ronksley et al. 2011 (prospective cohorts to September 2009; against non-drinkers as each study defined them, mostly current non-drinkers including former drinkers; each study's most-adjusted estimate, unadjusted for 8 of 84): any drinking, incident CHD RR 0.71 (0.66–0.77; 29 studies), CHD mortality 0.75 (0.68–0.81; 31), CVD mortality 0.75 (0.70–0.80; 21); I² 72.2%. By intake (under 2.5, 2.5–14.9, 15–29.9, 30–60, over 60 g/day): incident CHD 0.96 (0.86–1.06), 0.75 (0.65–0.88), 0.66 (0.59–0.75), 0.67 (0.56–0.79), 0.76 (0.52–1.09); CHD mortality 0.92 (0.80–1.06), 0.79 (0.73–0.86), 0.79 (0.71–0.88), 0.77 (0.72–0.83), 0.75 (0.63–0.89). Against lifetime abstainers: incident CHD 0.73 (0.61–0.88; 9 studies), CHD mortality 0.75 (0.66–0.85; 7), CVD mortality 0.82 (0.78–0.86; 9). Former drinkers (against non-drinkers by the table, against drinkers by the text): CHD mortality 1.31 (1.02–1.68), CVD mortality 1.48 (1.23–1.79), incident CHD 1.10 (0.91–1.33). Roerecke & Rehm 2012 (44 studies to April 2010; against lifetime abstainers; former drinkers excluded and mortality corrected for them): fully stratified studies at 2.5–11.99, 12–23.99, 24–35.99 g/day, men's IHD mortality 0.89 (0.79–1.00), 0.86 (0.73–1.02), 0.78 (0.63–0.97); men's morbidity 0.77 (0.65–0.92), 0.75 (0.64–0.88), 0.74 (0.53–1.02); women's mortality 0.84 (0.74–0.96), 1.03 (0.84–1.27), 0.89 (0.57–1.40); women's morbidity 0.54 (0.45–0.65), 0.61 (0.38–0.99), 0.40 (0.14–1.13); occasional drinking 0.82 to 0.98, none significant; all 44 studies 0.62 to 0.81, every interval excluding 1 (occasional 0.87 to 0.97, none significant); I² up to 84%. GBD 2016 (592 studies; against each study's non-drinking category, adjusted for former drinkers in it): IHD minimum RR 0.86 (95% UI 0.80–0.96) in men at 0.83 and 0.82 (0.72–0.95) in women at 0.92 standard drinks (10 g) a day; no significant dip for any other of 23 outcomes. UK Biobank (Biddinger et al. 2022): J- or U-shaped conventional associations; the moderate-intake difference for coronary artery disease not significant after six lifestyle factors (no values printed). China Kadoorie Biobank men (Millwood et al. 2019): conventional U shape for heart attack and CHD (no values printed for non-drinkers). Second-hand (Roerecke & Rehm 2014): former drinkers against lifetime abstainers, IHD mortality men 1.25 (1.15–1.36), women 1.54 (1.17–2.03); men drinking 60 g/day or more, IHD mortality 1.00 (0.74–1.36) against lifetime abstainers, against Ronksley et al.'s 0.75 (0.63–0.89) against current non-drinkers above 60 g/day. No absolute risks in any paper read.

claims.statement: In Chinese men and in people of European descent, genetically higher alcohol intake compared with genetically lower intake is associated with more stroke, most clearly with bleeding into the brain (intracerebral haemorrhage), and the Chinese study found no sign of a lower risk at low intake; cohort studies comparing people who drink with people who do not found no overall difference in stroke but more strokes at higher intakes. No paper read gives absolute risks of stroke by amount. In 161,498 genotyped Chinese adults from ten areas, followed about 10 years, men's stroke risk rose steadily across six groups whose genotypes and area predicted mean intakes of 4 to 256 g of ethanol a week: per 100 g a week (about 14 g a day, editors' arithmetic) ischaemic stroke 1.09 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.14; 5,709 cases), intracerebral haemorrhage 1.18 (1.12 to 1.24; 2,790 cases) and all stroke 1.12 (1.09 to 1.16); the lowest group, in which two thirds did not drink, showed no sign of a raised risk, and the next two groups (about 100 g a week) had higher, not lower, risk of ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage than the three lowest groups pooled (about 25 g a week); the same genotypes showed no association in women, few of whom drink (ischaemic stroke 0.98, 0.88 to 1.09; intracerebral haemorrhage 0.96, 0.82 to 1.12); and self-reported drinking in the same men showed a U shape, with lower stroke risk at about 100 g a week than in non-drinkers and former drinkers (Millwood et al., 2019). If, and only if, there is no protective effect and the relation is log-linear, those authors estimate that alcohol caused about 8 in 100 ischaemic strokes and 16 in 100 intracerebral haemorrhages among the men studied (a model estimate). In European-descent summary data the odds of stroke were 1.27 (1.12 to 1.45) per standard deviation of genetically predicted log drinks a week, 1.21 (1.05 to 1.40) after allowing for genetic liability to smoking; ischaemic stroke 1.26 (1.09 to 1.46) and intracerebral haemorrhage 3.53 (1.70 to 7.32) (Larsson et al., 2020); in UK Biobank, a genetic score for alcohol use disorder gave 1.26 (1.04 to 1.54), not significant at that paper's threshold for six outcomes (Biddinger et al., 2022). Carriers of the ADH1B variant, who reported 17% less drinking, had lower odds of ischaemic stroke in the studies with subtype data (0.83, 0.72 to 0.95) but no difference in all stroke (0.98, 0.90 to 1.07; 10,164 strokes) (Holmes et al., 2014). In cohort studies, people who drank had, against non-drinkers (most groups including former drinkers), no different risk of new stroke (0.98, 0.91 to 1.06; 17 studies) or of stroke death (1.06, 0.91 to 1.23; 10 studies), and against lifetime abstainers a higher risk of stroke death (1.29, 1.09 to 1.53; 3 studies); by intake, new strokes were less common at up to 14.9 g a day (0.81 and 0.80; 3 studies each) and more common above 60 g a day (1.62, 1.32 to 1.98; 4 studies) (Ronksley et al., 2011); in the GBD 2016 curves ischaemic stroke dipped at low intake without statistical significance. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Millwood et al. 2019 (China Kadoorie Biobank men; genetic, per 280 g/week of genotype-predicted mean intake): ischaemic stroke RR 1.27 (1.13–1.43; 5,709 cases), intracerebral haemorrhage 1.58 (1.36–1.84; 2,790), all stroke 1.38 (1.26–1.51; 9,189); per 100 g/week 1.09 (1.04–1.14), 1.18 (1.12–1.24), 1.12 (1.09–1.16); single variants (GG against AG) stroke 1.19 (1.13–1.24) rs671 and 1.19 (1.11–1.27) rs1229984; women ischaemic stroke 0.98 (0.88–1.09), intracerebral haemorrhage 0.96 (0.82–1.12); conventional, current drinkers per 280 g/week, 1.28 (1.19–1.38), 1.59 (1.37–1.85), 1.35 (1.27–1.44), with a U shape against non-drinkers (not printed); attributable shares if there is no protection and the relation is log-linear: about 8% of ischaemic strokes and 16% of intracerebral haemorrhages in men. Larsson et al. 2020 (per SD of genetically predicted log drinks/week): stroke OR 1.27 (1.12–1.45), adjusted for smoking liability 1.21 (1.05–1.40); ischaemic stroke 1.26 (1.09–1.46); intracerebral haemorrhage 3.53 (1.70–7.32); subarachnoid haemorrhage (UK Biobank) 2.47 (1.08–5.62); ADH1B variant alone ischaemic stroke 1.31 (1.05–1.65), intracerebral haemorrhage 11.5 (1.31–101.46). Biddinger et al. 2022: stroke 1.26 (1.04–1.54; P = .021, threshold P < .008). Holmes et al. 2014 (intake-lowering variant): all stroke 0.98 (0.90–1.07), ischaemic stroke 0.83 (0.72–0.95). Ronksley et al. 2011 (cohorts; against non-drinkers, mostly current): incident stroke 0.98 (0.91–1.06), stroke death 1.06 (0.91–1.23); against lifetime abstainers 0.93 (0.85–1.02) and 1.29 (1.09–1.53); incident stroke by intake (under 2.5 to over 60 g/day) 0.81, 0.80, 0.92, 1.15, 1.62 (1.32–1.98); haemorrhagic 1.14 (0.97–1.34), ischaemic 0.92 (0.85–1.00). No absolute risks in any paper read.
